A self-study course in seven lessons · Visual edition

The House of Timur

Its conquest of Persia and India, from Samarkand to the Mughals, c. 1336–1600

Prepared by Scholar · September 2026

This short course follows one family across roughly two and a half centuries. It starts with a minor Turkic-Mongol nobleman from the valley of Kesh who became the most feared conqueror of the late Middle Ages. It ends with his descendants ruling most of the Indian subcontinent from Agra and Delhi, still calling themselves "the house of Timur." Along the way it covers the wreck of Ilkhanid Persia, the sack of Delhi, the cultural flowering of Herat and Samarkand, and the long exile and comeback that turned a Central Asian prince into the first Mughal emperor.

Each lesson should take 20–30 minutes to read. Every lesson opens with a strip of key dates and a short "why it matters" note. It ends with a glossary of people and terms (with transliterations and, where useful, Persian or Chagatai script) and review questions whose answers open when you tap them. Contested figures, especially the death tolls at Isfahan and Delhi, are given as the chroniclers' claims and credited to them. They are not established facts.

About this edition. The maps are drawn from real geographic data (Natural Earth coastlines, rivers and lakes) with city positions from published coordinates. The historical borders come from an open dataset and are approximate. The charts use only dates from the lessons and published estimates, and every number is credited to its source. The data sources are listed at the end.

A note on names. Timur (Chagatai تیمور, Temür, "iron") is the same man as the European "Tamerlane," a corruption of the Persian Tīmūr-i lang, "Timur the Lame." Transliterations are simplified: Shah Rukh, not Shāhrukh; Navoi, not Navāʾī. Dates are CE.

Overview

The story at a glance

Three views of the whole period before the lessons begin: who ruled when, how far the family's realms reached at different dates, and how big those realms were according to the one systematic scholarly set of area estimates.

1Lesson 1

The world Timur was born into

1335–1379

Key dates
  1. 1335Death of the Ilkhan Abu Saʿid; Mongol Persia begins to fragment
  2. 1336Traditional date of Timur's birth near Kesh
  3. 1346–47Amir Qazaghan kills the khan Qazan; western Chagatai khans become figureheads
  4. 1360–61Tughluq Temür of Moghulistan invades Transoxiana
  5. c. 1363Timur wounded in Sistan and lamed
  6. 1370Fall of Amir Husayn at Balkh; Timur supreme in Transoxiana, capital at Samarkand
  7. 1379Khwarazm (Urgench) subdued
Why it matters

Timur's rise shows how politics worked in the ruins of the Mongol empire. With no Chinggisid blood, he ruled through a puppet khan and married into the royal line to become güregen, and Manz argues that he needed constant campaigning to keep his tribal army loyal. That explains the conquests in the next three lessons. The güregen title also gave the Mughal dynasty its own name, Gurkani.

In 1335 the last effective Mongol ruler of Persia, the Ilkhan Abu Saʿid, died without an heir, and the Ilkhanate began to break apart into local dynasties. According to the traditional date, Timur was born the following year, on 8 or 9 April 1336, near Kesh (today's Shahrisabz, "the green city") in the valley of the Qashqa Darya south of Samarkand. Beatrice Manz and other historians note that the date may have been adjusted later for astrological or symbolic reasons. Either way, it places his birth inside the ruins of the Mongol world order, and that order shaped everything he did.

The Chagatai Khanate

When Chinggis Khan divided his conquests among his sons, the second son, Chagatai, received the lands of Central Asia. They centred on Transoxiana, the settled, irrigated country between the Amu Darya (Oxus) and Syr Darya (Jaxartes), with its great cities of Samarkand and Bukhara, and they reached east into the steppe and the Tian Shan. By the 1340s this Chagatai Khanate had split in two. In the east, Moghulistan kept a more nomadic life and real Chinggisid khans. In the west, in Transoxiana, the tribal amirs (commanders) held the real power. In 1346–47 the amir Qazaghan killed the Chagatai khan Qazan, and after that the western khans were largely puppets. Military power lay with a handful of Turkic-speaking tribes: the Barlas, the Jalayir, the Suldus, the Arlat, and the Qaraʾunas.

The Barlas

Timur belonged to the Barlas. They were originally a Mongol tribe that had come west with Chagatai, but by the fourteenth century they spoke Turkic and were Muslim. Their home territory was the Kesh region. His father Taraghay was a respectable but minor figure, not a great chief. Timur's rise was therefore a personal achievement, won through the steppe politics of alliance, betrayal, raiding, and patronage. Manz has shown that his real talent lay in managing these tribal networks, winning followers personally loyal to him and then turning them against the old tribal leadership.

Rise to power, 1360–1370

The opportunity came when Tughluq Temür, the Chinggisid khan of Moghulistan, invaded Transoxiana in 1360 and 1361. Timur went over to him and was confirmed in control of Kesh. When the Moghuls withdrew, he allied with Amir Husayn, grandson of Qazaghan and leader of the Qaraʾunas, and married Husayn's sister. For most of the 1360s the two men were partners and rivals by turns. They fought the Moghuls together, fell out, and made up again. Around 1363, in fighting in Sistan, Timur took wounds to his right leg and right arm that lamed him for life. That is the origin of the Persian nickname Tīmūr-i lang. In 1941 Soviet scientists led by Mikhail Gerasimov opened his tomb, and his skeleton showed injuries consistent with these accounts.

By 1370 Timur had outmanoeuvred Husayn. Husayn was besieged at Balkh, surrendered, and was killed. That spring a gathering (quriltai) at Balkh acknowledged Timur as supreme amir of the Chagatai ulus, and he made Samarkand his capital.

Why "güregen" and not "khan"

After Balkh, Timur married Saray Mulk Khanum, one of Husayn's widows and a daughter of the Chagatai khan Qazan, a Chinggisid princess. The marriage gave him the title güregen (Persian gūrkān), "royal son-in-law." The title mattered because across the post-Mongol world only a descendant of Chinggis Khan in the male line could legitimately be khan. Timur was not one. So he never claimed the title. He ruled as amīr and güregen, and he kept a Chinggisid puppet khan on the throne: first Soyurghatmish, then his son Sultan Mahmud. Decrees were issued in the khan's name, and the army belonged to Timur.

This double legitimacy, Mongol and Islamic, ran through his whole career. He honoured the Chinggisid order and the steppe law and custom associated with it (the yasa). At the same time he presented himself as a Muslim ruler, patronised Sufi shaykhs and scholars, and let his historians call him ṣāḥib-qirān, "Lord of the Auspicious Conjunction," a title with astrological and messianic overtones. His spiritual guide, Mir Sayyid Baraka, would eventually be buried at his feet. The güregen title also outlived him. His descendants in India called their dynasty the Gurkani, and that is a thread this course will follow to the end.

Consolidation in the 1370s

The 1370s were spent securing the base. Timur campaigned repeatedly against Moghulistan to the east and against Khwarazm, the rich oasis on the lower Oxus, which he finally subdued by 1379. He also began a policy he kept for the rest of his life: keeping the tribal army busy and rewarded through constant campaigns abroad, so that its energies were not turned against him at home. As Manz argues, conquest was not only Timur's ambition. It was also how his regime held together. By 1380 he was ready to look south-west, across the Oxus, to the fragments of Mongol Persia.

Key people and terms

Timur / Temür تیمور
"Iron." Founder of the dynasty (1336–1405). Called Tīmūr-i lang تیمور لنگ, "the Lame," which became "Tamerlane."
Barlas برلاس
Turkicised Mongol tribe of the Kesh region; Timur's tribe.
Ulus اولوس
A people or polity under a ruler; the "Chagatai ulus" is the realm and its tribal army.
Amir امیر
Commander. Timur's own title (amīr-i kabīr, "great amir").
Güregen / Gūrkān گورکان
"Royal son-in-law." Title from marriage into the house of Chinggis Khan; root of the Mughals' dynastic name, Gūrkāniyān.
Amir Husayn
Qaraʾunas leader, Timur's ally and rival; killed at Balkh in 1370.
Saray Mulk Khanum
Chinggisid princess, daughter of the khan Qazan; Timur's senior wife.
Ṣāḥib-qirān صاحب‌قران
"Lord of the Auspicious Conjunction." Honorific later reused by Shah Jahan as "the Second Sahib-qiran."
Yasa یاسا
The body of law and custom attributed to Chinggis Khan.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1Why could Timur not call himself khan, and what did he do instead?
Answer. Only male-line descendants of Chinggis Khan could legitimately be khan. Timur ruled as amīr, kept puppet Chinggisid khans (Soyurghatmish, then Sultan Mahmud), and married a Chinggisid princess to become güregen, "royal son-in-law."
2What was the political difference between Moghulistan and western (Transoxianan) Chagatai territory by the 1350s?
Answer. Moghulistan in the east kept real Chinggisid khans and a more nomadic life. In Transoxiana the tribal amirs held power and the khans were figureheads, especially after Qazaghan killed Qazan in 1346–47.
3How did Timur use the invasions of Tughluq Temür to advance his career?
Answer. He submitted to Tughluq Temür and was confirmed in control of Kesh, then used that base to ally with Amir Husayn once the Moghuls withdrew.
4According to Manz, why was continual foreign campaigning structurally important to Timur's regime?
Answer. Constant campaigns kept the tribal army occupied, rewarded, and loyal to him personally. Conquest held the regime together and kept rivals from turning on him.

2Lesson 2

The conquest of Persia, 1380s–1390s

1380–1396

Key dates
  1. 1381Herat submits; Kartid ruler Pir ʿAli becomes a tributary
  2. 1383Herat revolt crushed; Sistan and Kandahar campaigns
  3. 1385Tokhtamysh sacks Tabriz
  4. 1386–88The "three-year campaign": Tabriz, Georgia, Isfahan and Shiraz (1387)
  5. 1391Victory over Tokhtamysh at the Kondurcha River
  6. 1392–96The "five-year campaign": end of the Muzaffarids and Baghdad (1393), the Terek (1395), sack of Sarai
Why it matters

Persia made Timur rich. It supplied the treasure and the deported craftsmen who built Samarkand, it set the pattern of ransom for cities that submitted and massacre for cities that resisted, and it brought Herat, the future Timurid capital, into the family's hands. The wars with Tokhtamysh also did lasting damage to the Golden Horde, which historians note indirectly helped Muscovy.

When Timur crossed the Oxus in 1380–81, Iran was a patchwork of successor states that had grown up after the Ilkhanate collapsed. The Kartids ruled Herat. The Sarbadars, a mix of local notables and Shiʿi-leaning dervishes, held Sabzavar in western Khorasan. The Muzaffarids ruled Fars, Kirman, and Isfahan from Shiraz. The Jalayirids, Mongols by origin, held Baghdad and, at times, Tabriz. None of them could withstand Timur's army, and they fought one another as much as him. His conquest of Persia came in a series of campaigns that later Timurid historians named by their length: the "three-year" campaign (1386–88), the "five-year" campaign (1392–96), and the "seven-year" campaign (1399–1404).

Herat and Khorasan

The first target was Herat. In 1381 the Kartid ruler Ghiyath al-Din Pir ʿAli submitted with little resistance. Timur took the city's treasures, had its walls pulled down, and sent notables and artisans north to Kesh and Samarkand. When Herat rebelled in 1383, the revolt was crushed, and within a few years the Kartid princes had been put to death. The Sarbadars of Sabzavar also submitted, and when Sabzavar later rose, Timur's chroniclers boast that he had prisoners built alive into towers. He campaigned in Sistan and took Kandahar in 1383, and by the mid-1380s the whole of Khorasan was his. Herat's later role as the second Timurid capital began with this conquest.

The three-year campaign and Isfahan, 1387

In 1386 Timur moved west through northern Iran to Tabriz and on into Georgia and eastern Anatolia. In 1387 he turned south to Isfahan, which belonged to the Muzaffarids. The city surrendered, and a ransom was agreed. Then, during the night, the townspeople rose and killed the Timurid officials and soldiers who had been sent in to collect it. The retaliation was one of the most notorious episodes of his career. Each unit of the army was ordered to deliver a quota of heads, and the heads were piled into towers outside the walls. The Timurid historian Hafiz-i Abru claimed to have seen and counted them and gives about 70,000 dead, the figure repeated in the Encyclopaedia Iranica. Later accounts, some much later, give larger numbers. No figure can be checked, and chronicle totals of this kind often served to magnify the conqueror. What is not in doubt is that the massacre was deliberate, organised, and meant to be remembered.

Shiraz, the Muzaffarids, and Hafez

Shiraz, the Muzaffarid capital, submitted in 1387. Timur installed the Muzaffarid princes as tributaries and withdrew. He had to, because his old protégé Tokhtamysh was raiding Transoxiana. A famous story belongs to this first stay at Shiraz. The poet Hafez had written a ghazal offering Samarkand and Bukhara for the mole on a beloved's cheek. Timur is said to have summoned him and asked how he dared give away the conqueror's cities for a mole. Hafez supposedly bowed, pointed to his threadbare clothes, and said that such generosity was why he had come to this poverty. The story first appears in Dawlatshah Samarqandi's biographical dictionary of poets, written in 1487, a century after the supposed meeting. It is almost certainly legend. It is still worth knowing as a sign of how later Persian culture imagined the encounter between the sword and the pen.

In 1393, during the five-year campaign, Timur came back to finish the Muzaffarids. Shah Mansur, the most capable of them, led a daring charge outside Shiraz that reportedly came close to reaching Timur himself before he was killed. The surviving Muzaffarid princes were executed soon afterwards, and Fars was given to Timurid princes.

Baghdad and the Jalayirids

In August 1393 Timur took Baghdad. The Jalayirid sultan Ahmad fled west to the Mamluks of Egypt and Syria, and there he would keep reappearing as a nuisance. Baghdad was not held for long, and in 1401 Timur came back and sacked it with great bloodshed (Lesson 4). The Jalayirid episode shows a pattern. Timur could beat any army in the region, but he did not always build lasting administration in the places he conquered, so some cities had to be taken twice.

The war with Tokhtamysh

Tokhtamysh was a Chinggisid prince of the Jochid line whom Timur had sheltered and helped to power in the 1370s. As khan of the Golden Horde he turned on his patron. He sacked Tabriz in 1385 and raided Transoxiana while Timur was away in Iran. Timur answered with two huge steppe expeditions. In 1391 he marched north across the Kazakh steppe and defeated Tokhtamysh at the Kondurcha River, near the Volga. In 1395 he won again at the Terek River in the northern Caucasus and then sacked the Horde's commercial cities, including its capital Sarai on the lower Volga and Astrakhan. These campaigns did lasting damage to the Golden Horde and to the northern trade routes it controlled. Historians often note that this indirectly helped Muscovy.

Methods: terror, deportation, and tribute

Timur's methods were calculated. A city that submitted quickly usually paid a large ransom (māl-i amān, "protection money") and was spared. A city that resisted, or rebelled after submitting as Isfahan did, could expect massacre, towers of heads, and the destruction of its walls. The towers were propaganda as much as punishment, a message for the next city. Almost everywhere he took skilled craftsmen: builders, weavers, tile-makers, and scholars were deported to Samarkand and Kesh, and they built the monuments of his capital. Conquered lands were entrusted to his sons and grandsons, supported by Persian bureaucrats who assessed and collected revenue. Miran Shah was given the north-west around Tabriz, ʿUmar Shaykh and then his son Pir Muhammad got Fars, and Shah Rukh got Herat in 1397. The system produced enormous wealth for Samarkand. It also produced a realm held together mainly by Timur himself.

Key people and terms

Kartids آل کرت
Dynasty of Herat (1245–1380s), vassals of the Ilkhans.
Sarbadars سربداران
"Heads on the gallows." Rulers of Sabzavar in western Khorasan.
Muzaffarids آل مظفر
Dynasty of Fars, Kirman, and Isfahan with its capital at Shiraz; ended in 1393.
Jalayirids جلایریان
Mongol successor dynasty in Baghdad and Tabriz; Sultan Ahmad Jalayir.
Tokhtamysh توقتمش
Khan of the Golden Horde, Timur's protégé turned enemy.
Hafez حافظ
Shams al-Din Muhammad Hafez of Shiraz (d. 1389/90), the great lyric poet.
Hafiz-i Abru حافظ ابرو
Timurid court historian (d. 1430); source of the 70,000 figure for Isfahan.
Māl-i amān مال امان
"Security money." The ransom a submitting city paid to be spared.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1Name the four main successor states of the Ilkhanate that Timur faced in Iran and where each was based.
Answer. The Kartids (Herat), the Sarbadars (Sabzavar), the Muzaffarids (Shiraz, with Fars, Kirman, and Isfahan), and the Jalayirids (Baghdad and Tabriz).
2What happened at Isfahan in 1387, and how should the figure of 70,000 dead be treated?
Answer. Isfahan surrendered, then rose at night and killed the Timurid collectors. Timur ordered a massacre and towers of heads. The 70,000 figure comes from the court historian Hafiz-i Abru. It should be credited to him as a chronicler's claim, not treated as a verified count.
3What is the source of the Timur–Hafez anecdote, and why do historians doubt it?
Answer. It first appears in Dawlatshah Samarqandi's anthology of 1487, a century later. It is too neat and too late to be trusted.
4How did Timur's treatment of submitting and resisting cities differ, and what did he take from both?
Answer. Cities that submitted paid ransom (māl-i amān) and were generally spared. Cities that resisted or rebelled faced massacre and destruction. From both he took treasure and, especially, skilled artisans deported to Samarkand and Kesh.

3Lesson 3

The Indian campaign of 1398–99

1398–1451

Key dates
  1. 1347Bahmani sultanate founded in the Deccan
  2. 1388Death of Firuz Shah Tughluq; succession crisis in Delhi
  3. 1394Jaunpur becomes effectively independent
  4. 1397–98Pir Muhammad besieges Multan
  5. Sept 1398Timur crosses the Indus
  6. 17 Dec 1398Defeat of Mahmud Shah Tughluq and Mallu Iqbal outside Delhi; sack follows
  7. Mar 1399Timur recrosses the Indus
  8. c. 1401–07Malwa and Gujarat become independent sultanates
  9. 1414Khizr Khan takes Delhi; Sayyid dynasty
  10. 1451Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi dynasty
Why it matters

Timur spent only about six months in India, but he broke what was left of the Delhi Sultanate's power and opened the age of the regional sultanates. Delhi briefly became, in form, a Timurid dependency when Khizr Khan acknowledged Shah Rukh. That gave the house of Timur a claim to India, and Babur revived it 127 years later.

Timur's invasion of India lasted barely six months, and he never tried to govern the country. It still had consequences out of all proportion to its length. It broke what was left of the Delhi Sultanate's power, sped up the rise of regional sultanates across North India, and left a claim, remembered in family tradition, that Babur would revive 127 years later.

A sultanate in decline

Under Muhammad bin Tughluq (r. 1325–51) the Delhi Sultanate reached its greatest extent, but it was already fraying at the edges. Bengal and the Deccan had broken away by the 1340s, the Deccan under the new Bahmani dynasty (1347). His successor Firuz Shah Tughluq (r. 1351–88) ruled a smaller but fairly stable realm. After Firuz died in 1388, a series of short reigns, palace coups, and factional wars followed. By the mid-1390s there were two rival sultans, Nasir al-Din Mahmud Shah and Nusrat Shah, holding different quarters of the Delhi complex. Real power belonged to the noble Mallu Iqbal Khan. In 1394 the eunuch governor Malik Sarwar made himself effectively independent at Jaunpur in the east. To an outside predator, Delhi was rich, famous, and badly defended.

Pretexts and preparations

Timur's historian Sharaf al-Din ʿAli Yazdi, who finished his Zafarnāma (Book of Victory) in the 1420s, frames the campaign as a holy war against rulers who were too lenient toward their Hindu subjects. Historians generally treat this as justification after the fact. The more obvious motives were plunder and prestige, and Delhi was among the richest cities in the Islamic world. In 1397–98 Timur's grandson Pir Muhammad was sent ahead and besieged Multan. Timur himself left Samarkand in the spring of 1398, went through the Hindu Kush by way of Kabul, and crossed the Indus in September 1398.

The march on Delhi

The army moved through the Punjab, sacking Tulamba and then the fortress of Bhatnair (Bhatner) on the edge of the Thar desert, and reached the outskirts of Delhi in December. By then it was carrying a huge crowd of captives taken along the way. Before the battle, according to Yazdi, Timur ordered them killed, fearing they would rise or join the enemy once fighting began. Yazdi gives the number as 100,000. That figure comes from a court history written to glorify its hero. Modern historians accept that a large massacre of prisoners took place but treat the number as uncertain and probably inflated. The episode is best read as an attested atrocity of unknown size.

The battle and the sack

On 17 December 1398 the army of Mahmud Shah and Mallu Iqbal came out to fight. It included war elephants, which unsettled Timur's troops. The chroniclers describe ditches, caltrops, and other defences prepared against the elephants. The Delhi army was routed. Mahmud Shah fled towards Gujarat, and Mallu Iqbal fled to Baran. The city's notables submitted and a ransom was agreed. Then things went badly wrong. The sources describe clashes between Timurid soldiers collecting the levy and the townspeople, and the collection turned into a general sack that went on for several days across Delhi's several walled cities: Siri, Jahanpanah, and Old Delhi. Huge numbers of people were killed or enslaved. Whether Timur ordered the sack or let it happen after his troops got out of hand, the Timurid sources themselves admit it happened, and later Indian writers remembered it as a catastrophe. As with Isfahan, reliable totals do not exist. Figures in the tens of thousands or more appear in the chronicles and in modern popular works, and they should be credited to their sources, not repeated as fact.

Timur then took what he wanted. Stonemasons and other craftsmen were marched back to Samarkand, where they worked on the great congregational mosque now called Bibi-Khanym. Elephants and treasure followed. He did not linger. He struck north-east to Meerut and then to Haridwar on the Ganges, skirted the Siwalik hills, passed through Jammu, and recrossed the Indus in March 1399. In Delhi's northern countryside, the Indian historian Yahya Sirhindi (writing in the 1430s) recorded famine and pestilence in the wake of the army.

After the storm: North India fragments

The Tughluq dynasty survived in name. Mahmud Shah came back to Delhi and lived until 1412, but he ruled little beyond it. Before leaving, Timur had entrusted Multan and the western Punjab to Khizr Khan, a noble who had joined him. In 1414 Khizr Khan took Delhi and founded the Sayyid dynasty. Tellingly, he did not take the title of sultan and at first acknowledged Timur's son Shah Rukh as overlord. So for a short time Delhi was, formally, a Timurid dependency. That fact would later strengthen Mughal claims. The Sayyids gave way in 1451 to the Afghan Lodis, whose last sultan, Ibrahim, would face Babur at Panipat.

The provinces went their own way. The Sharqi sultans of Jaunpur (from 1394) built a brilliant court in the east. Zafar Khan, governor of Gujarat, declared independence as Muzaffar Shah around 1407, and Gujarat became one of the richest sultanates in India. Malwa, under Dilawar Khan Ghuri and his son Hushang Shah, became independent around 1401–07 with its capital at Mandu. In the south, the Bahmani sultanate and the Hindu empire of Vijayanagara went on with their rivalry. For anyone who studies maps of India, the fifteenth century is the age of the regional sultanates, and Timur's raid is its opening act.

Key people and terms

Tughluqs تغلق
Delhi dynasty (1320–1413/14).
Nasir al-Din Mahmud Shah
Tughluq sultan defeated by Timur; d. 1412.
Mallu Iqbal Khan
Power behind the Delhi throne in the 1390s.
Sharaf al-Din ʿAli Yazdi شرف‌الدین علی یزدی
Author of the Zafarnāma ظفرنامه (completed 1420s), the official life of Timur.
Pir Muhammad b. Jahangir
Timur's grandson; led the advance guard in India and was Timur's designated heir.
Khizr Khan خضر خان
Founder of the Sayyid dynasty of Delhi (1414–51); acknowledged Timurid overlordship.
Regional sultanates
Jaunpur (Sharqi), Gujarat (Muzaffarid), Malwa (Ghuri/Khalji), Bengal, and the Bahmanis of the Deccan.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1What internal conditions made the Delhi Sultanate vulnerable in 1398?
Answer. After Firuz Shah died in 1388 came a succession crisis, rival sultans, domination by Mallu Iqbal, and provinces such as Jaunpur breaking away.
2What does Yazdi say happened to the captives before the battle of Delhi, and how should the figure be handled?
Answer. Yazdi says Timur had the captives killed before the battle, giving 100,000. Treat it as an attested massacre whose size comes from a court panegyric and is uncertain.
3Why is the Sayyid dynasty significant for the later Mughal claim to India?
Answer. Khizr Khan, Timur's appointee, founded it and acknowledged Shah Rukh as overlord. This made Delhi formally a Timurid dependency and strengthened Babur's later claim.
4Name three regional sultanates that flourished in North India after the invasion.
Answer. Any three of: Jaunpur (Sharqi), Gujarat, Malwa, Bengal, and in the south the Bahmanis.

4Lesson 4

The last campaigns and Timur's death

1399–1409

Key dates
  1. 1399Bibi-Khanym mosque begun; start of the "seven-year campaign"
  2. 1400Sack of Aleppo
  3. 1401Damascus taken; meeting with Ibn Khaldun; second sack of Baghdad
  4. 28 July 1402Battle of Ankara; Bayezid I captured
  5. Dec 1402Smyrna taken from the Knights Hospitaller
  6. 1402–13Ottoman Interregnum
  7. Sept–Nov 1404Clavijo's embassy at Samarkand
  8. 18 Feb 1405Timur dies at Otrar
  9. 1409Shah Rukh master of Transoxiana; Ulugh Beg governor of Samarkand
Why it matters

The victory at Ankara threw the Ottomans into a decade of civil war and delayed their advance on Constantinople by about fifty years. Ibn Khaldun and Clavijo left the best eyewitness portraits of Timur. His death at Otrar started a succession struggle that reshaped the dynasty, and the Gur-e Amir became the model for Humayun's tomb and, more distantly, the Taj Mahal.

Timur came home from India in 1399 aged about sixty-three. He rested only a few months. That autumn he set out on the last and longest of his western expeditions, the "seven-year campaign." It took him into Syria, against the Ottomans, and to the Aegean coast, and he returned to Samarkand only in 1404, to prepare for the invasion of China.

Syria and Baghdad, 1400–1401

Timur's quarrel with the Mamluk sultanate of Egypt and Syria had several causes. The Mamluks had sheltered Ahmad Jalayir, had executed one of his envoys, and held the cities of the Fertile Crescent. In October 1400 he took Aleppo. Damascus fell in early 1401 after negotiations that went sour, and it was plundered and burned, including damage to the Umayyad Mosque. The great North African historian Ibn Khaldun, who was then in Damascus, was let down from the city walls to meet Timur and later wrote an account of their conversations. It is one of the most valuable firsthand portraits of the conqueror, showing him curious about history and geography and questioning Ibn Khaldun closely about the Maghrib. In summer 1401 Timur returned to Baghdad, which had slipped back into Jalayirid hands, stormed it, and ordered another massacre with towers of heads. Chroniclers put the dead in the tens of thousands. Justin Marozzi, following the sources, repeats a figure of 90,000, and like the others it should be treated as a chronicler's claim.

Ankara, 1402

The Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, nicknamed Yıldırım ("Thunderbolt"), had been expanding into eastern Anatolia, where Timur claimed overlordship over local Turkmen lords. For several years the two sovereigns traded insulting letters. The Ottomans also gave shelter to Timur's enemies, including the Qara Qoyunlu Turkmen chief Qara Yusuf. On 28 July 1402 the armies met near Ankara. Several Anatolian contingents in Bayezid's army, whose former lords were riding with Timur, changed sides during the battle. Bayezid's Serbian allies fought hard, but the Ottoman army collapsed. Bayezid was captured and died in captivity at Akşehir in March 1403. The famous story that Timur kept him in an iron cage comes from later sources and is disputed. It may come from a misunderstanding of a barred litter, and it is best treated as legend. That December Timur also took Smyrna (Izmir) from the Knights Hospitaller, a victory his historians used to present him as a warrior for Islam.

The consequences were large. The Ottoman state fell into a decade-long civil war among Bayezid's sons, the Interregnum of 1402–13. It survived, but its advance on Constantinople was delayed by half a century. European rulers, hoping for an ally against the Turks, sent envoys to the new power in the east.

Clavijo at Samarkand

One of those envoys was Ruy González de Clavijo, sent by King Henry III of Castile. He reached Samarkand in September 1404 and stayed until November. His account, available in English as Embassy to Tamerlane, 1403–1406, is the best Western eyewitness description of Timur's capital. He describes garden palaces outside the walls, feasts on a staggering scale, envoys from as far as China, and the great congregational mosque going up under the old ruler's impatient eye. Clavijo saw Timur himself as an old man with failing eyesight who still commanded completely.

The mosque of Bibi-Khanym

That mosque, begun in 1399 with the spoils and captive masons of India, was meant to outdo anything in the Islamic east. Its entrance portal and main dome were colossal. The name Bibi-Khanym ("the senior lady") came to be linked with Saray Mulk Khanum, although the stories about her building it are legends. Built too quickly and too big, the mosque began to crumble soon after its completion. It stood as a picturesque ruin for centuries and has been heavily restored since the Soviet period.

The China campaign and death at Otrar

Timur's last project was the conquest of Ming China. The Hongwu emperor had treated him in diplomatic letters as a tributary, which he resented, and he detained Ming envoys at his court. In the winter of 1404–05 he set out eastward with a huge army. It was an extraordinary decision for a man near seventy to make in midwinter. At Otrar on the Syr Darya he fell ill, and he died there on 18 February 1405. The China campaign was called off.

The succession crisis Timur had tried to prevent broke out at once. His designated heir, the grandson Pir Muhammad b. Jahangir, was far away in Kandahar. Another grandson, Khalil Sultan, son of Miran Shah, seized Samarkand and the treasury. Pir Muhammad was murdered in 1407. By 1409 Timur's youngest surviving son, Shah Rukh, ruling from Herat, had made himself master of Transoxiana and installed his own son Ulugh Beg at Samarkand. The western conquests, including Azerbaijan, Iraq, and eastern Anatolia, were largely lost to the Turkmen confederations within a few years.

Gur-e Amir

Timur was buried in Samarkand in the Gur-e Amir ("Tomb of the Amir"), a domed complex he had begun for his favourite grandson and heir-apparent Muhammad Sultan, who died in 1403. Its ribbed, melon-shaped turquoise dome on a tall drum became a model for later Timurid and Mughal tombs, and its descendants include Humayun's tomb in Delhi and, more distantly, the Taj Mahal. Inside, Timur lies under a cenotaph of dark green jade (nephrite), placed there by Ulugh Beg in the 1420s. Near him lie his sons Shah Rukh and Miran Shah, his grandsons Muhammad Sultan and Ulugh Beg, and his spiritual guide Mir Sayyid Baraka. In June 1941 Gerasimov's team opened the tomb. A popular story links the opening to the German invasion of the Soviet Union days later, but that is folklore, not history.

Key people and terms

Bayezid I Yıldırım
Ottoman sultan (r. 1389–1402), defeated and captured at Ankara.
Ibn Khaldun ابن خلدون
Historian (1332–1406), author of the Muqaddima; met Timur at Damascus in 1401.
Ruy González de Clavijo
Castilian envoy (d. 1412) whose embassy account describes Samarkand in 1404.
Bibi-Khanym بی‌بی خانم
Timur's congregational mosque in Samarkand.
Gur-e Amir گور امیر
"Tomb of the Amir," Timur's mausoleum.
Khalil Sultan
Grandson (son of Miran Shah) who seized Samarkand in 1405; displaced by 1409.
Shah Rukh شاهرخ
Timur's youngest son (1377–1447), ruler from Herat.
Otrar اترار
Town on the Syr Darya where Timur died; famous as the place where the Khwarazmshah's governor massacred Chinggis Khan's caravan in 1218.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1What were the causes and the most important consequence of the battle of Ankara?
Answer. The causes were rival claims over the eastern Anatolian lords and Ottoman sheltering of Timur's enemies such as Qara Yusuf. The most important consequence was the Ottoman Interregnum (1402–13), which delayed the fall of Constantinople by about fifty years.
2Why are Ibn Khaldun and Clavijo so valuable as sources on Timur?
Answer. Both are firsthand outsiders: Ibn Khaldun met and questioned Timur at Damascus, and Clavijo described Samarkand and the aged conqueror in 1404.
3Why did Timur's death at Otrar lead immediately to a succession crisis, and who emerged as ruler?
Answer. His designated heir Pir Muhammad was far away in Kandahar, and Khalil Sultan seized Samarkand. By 1409 Shah Rukh had won out.
4Name two architectural features of the Gur-e Amir and one later monument it influenced.
Answer. A ribbed, melon-shaped dome on a high drum and turquoise tilework, with a dark green jade cenotaph inside. It influenced Humayun's tomb (and, more distantly, the Taj Mahal).

5Lesson 5

Successors and the "Timurid Renaissance"

1405–1510

Key dates
  1. 1405/1409–47Reign of Shah Rukh, based at Herat
  2. 1417–20Ulugh Beg's madrasa on the Registan, Samarkand
  3. 1418Gawhar Shad mosque at Mashhad completed
  4. 1420sUlugh Beg's observatory built
  5. 1430Baysunghur Shahnama
  6. c. 1437Zīj-i Sulṭānī completed
  7. 1449Ulugh Beg killed on his son's orders
  8. 1467Uzun Hasan (Aq Qoyunlu) defeats Jahan Shah (Qara Qoyunlu)
  9. 1469Abu Saʿid defeated and killed; Husayn Bayqara takes Herat
  10. 1499Navoi's Muḥākamat al-lughatayn
  11. 1500–01Shaybani Khan takes Samarkand
  12. 1506–07Death of Husayn Bayqara; Uzbeks take Herat
  13. 1510Shah Ismaʿil defeats and kills Shaybani near Merv
Why it matters

Politically, the fifteenth-century Timurids kept losing ground. Culturally, they set the standard for the whole Persianate world. Herat painting, Ulugh Beg's astronomy, Navoi's Chagatai poetry and the Timurid style of architecture were copied by the Safavids, the Ottomans and the Mughals. The Uzbek conquest then pushed the dynasty south of the Hindu Kush, towards India.

Timur conquered, and his descendants patronised. Over the fifteenth century the Timurid princes lost most of their grandfather's empire, yet they presided over one of the great flowerings of Persianate culture. Painting, calligraphy, poetry in Persian and Turkic, astronomy, and architecture set standards that the Safavids, Ottomans, and Mughals would all imitate. Historians borrow the word "renaissance" for this period with some caution, but it is hard to find a better one.

Shah Rukh and Gawhar Shad at Herat

Shah Rukh ruled from 1405 (and over Transoxiana from 1409) until his death in 1447. He was a very different sovereign from his father: pious, cautious, and more interested in keeping what he had than in conquest, though he did campaign three times against the Qara Qoyunlu in Azerbaijan. He made Herat his capital, and under him it became the cultural centre of the eastern Islamic world. Beatrice Manz's Power, Politics and Religion in Timurid Iran is a study of how his regime actually worked. It relied on alliances among Turkic amirs, Persian bureaucrats, city notables, ulama, and Sufi shaykhs.

His wife Gawhar Shad was one of the great patrons of Islamic architecture. At Mashhad she built the congregational mosque that bears her name, beside the shrine of Imam Reza, completed in 1418 by the architect Qavam al-Din Shirazi. At Herat she built a madrasa and mausoleum complex, the Musalla, whose surviving minarets still stand. She remained a political force long after her husband's death and was executed in 1457, in her eighties, during the struggles among his descendants. Their son Baysunghur (d. 1433) ran a celebrated royal workshop (kitābkhāna) of calligraphers, illuminators, and painters. Its most famous product is the Baysunghur Shahnama of 1430.

Ulugh Beg, the astronomer-prince

Shah Rukh's eldest son Ulugh Beg (1394–1449) governed Samarkand for almost forty years. On the Registan square he built a madrasa (1417–20) where mathematics and astronomy were taught alongside religious learning. In the 1420s, on a hill north-east of the city, he built an observatory whose centrepiece was a giant meridian arc, the lower part of which was dug into the rock and survives. With the astronomers Qadizada Rumi, Ghiyath al-Din Jamshid al-Kashi, and later ʿAli Qushji, he produced the Zīj-i Sulṭānī, completed around 1437. It is a set of astronomical tables with a star catalogue of 1,018 stars, the first major independent star catalogue since Ptolemy and the most accurate before Tycho Brahe. Ulugh Beg was a poor politician. When his father died in 1447 he became supreme ruler, but in 1449 he was defeated by his own son ʿAbd al-Latif and put to death on his orders. ʿAbd al-Latif himself was murdered a few months later.

Husayn Bayqara, Jami, and Navoi

The last brilliant Timurid court was that of Sultan Husayn Bayqara, a great-great-grandson of Timur through ʿUmar Shaykh, who ruled Herat from 1469 until his death in 1506. His Herat was a city of poets, painters, musicians, and scholars. Babur, who visited just after Husayn died, admired it and also found it decadent. Two figures dominate its literature. ʿAbd al-Rahman Jami (1414–1492), a Naqshbandi Sufi, was the last great classical Persian poet, author of the seven-poem Haft Awrang and of works on mysticism. His friend and patron ʿAli-Shir Navoi (1441–1501), Husayn's companion and minister, wrote in Persian but above all in Chagatai Turkic, the literary Turkic of the Timurid realm. His Muḥākamat al-lughatayn ("Judgement of the Two Languages," 1499) argued that Turkic was as fit as Persian for high literature. Navoi is honoured today as the founding figure of Uzbek literature. Chagatai is also the language in which Babur would write his memoirs.

Bihzad and Persian painting

Kamal al-Din Bihzad (c. 1450s–1535), who worked in Husayn Bayqara's library under Navoi's patronage, is the most celebrated name in Persian painting. His work, and work attributed to him, is known for tightly composed scenes full of individual, busy, often humorous figures: builders, servants, dervishes. The illustration of the Samarkand mosque under construction in Lesson 3 is typical of the manner linked to him. After Herat fell, Bihzad moved to the Safavid court at Tabriz, where Shah Ismaʿil appointed him head of the royal library in 1522. The painters of Humayun's and Akbar's studios were trained in that Safavid tradition, which is one of the direct lines from Herat to Mughal India.

Architecture

Timurid buildings are recognisable at a glance. They have monumental entrance portals (pīshṭāq), vast iwans, ribbed double-shell domes on tall drums, and surfaces sheathed in glazed tile: cut-tile mosaic, glazed brick patterns, and banna'i script. Samarkand's Shah-i Zinda necropolis, Timur's Aq Saray palace at Shahrisabz, the Gur-e Amir, Bibi-Khanym, Ulugh Beg's madrasa, and Gawhar Shad's buildings at Mashhad and Herat together make up a coherent style. It passed on to the Safavids at Isfahan and to the Mughals in India.

Fragmentation and rivals

Politically, the century after Timur was one of shrinking borders. In the west, two Turkmen confederations took over. The Qara Qoyunlu ("Black Sheep") under Qara Yusuf recovered Tabriz soon after Timur's death, and under Jahan Shah (r. 1438–67) they overran western and central Iran, even briefly occupying Herat in 1458. The Aq Qoyunlu ("White Sheep") of Diyarbakır, under Uzun Hasan, destroyed Jahan Shah in 1467. In 1469 Uzun Hasan defeated and captured the Timurid Abu Saʿid, who had briefly reunited Transoxiana and Khorasan, and Abu Saʿid was put to death. After that the Timurids held only the east. The Aq Qoyunlu were in turn swept away after 1501 by the young Shah Ismaʿil, founder of the Safavid dynasty.

The final blow came from the north. Muhammad Shaybani Khan, a Chinggisid of the Jochid line, led the Uzbek tribes south from the steppe. He took Samarkand in 1500–01, expelling the young Babur, and Herat in 1507, ending the line of Husayn Bayqara. Shaybani himself was defeated and killed by Shah Ismaʿil near Merv in 1510, but the Uzbek Shaybanids kept Transoxiana. The Timurid homeland was lost for good. The dynasty's future now lay south of the Hindu Kush.

Key people and terms

Baysunghur بایسنغر
Son of Shah Rukh; bibliophile patron (d. 1433).
Ulugh Beg الغ بیگ
"Great prince." Muhammad Taraghay, ruler of Samarkand and astronomer.
Zīj-i Sulṭānī زیج سلطانی
Ulugh Beg's astronomical tables and star catalogue.
Husayn Bayqara حسین بایقرا
Last great Timurid sultan of Herat (r. 1469–1506).
Jami جامی
ʿAbd al-Rahman Jami, Persian poet and Sufi (1414–1492).
Navoi علیشیر نوایی
ʿAli-Shir Navaʾi, Chagatai Turkic poet and statesman (1441–1501).
Chagatai (Turki)

Bihzad کمال‌الدین بهزاد

Qara Qoyunlu قره‌قویونلو / Aq Qoyunlu آق‌قویونلو

Shaybani Khan شیبانی خان

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1What were Ulugh Beg's main scientific achievements, and how did his reign end?
Answer. He built the Samarkand observatory with its giant meridian arc and produced the Zīj-i Sulṭānī with a catalogue of 1,018 stars. He was defeated and put to death on the orders of his son ʿAbd al-Latif in 1449.
2What did Navoi argue in the Muḥākamat al-lughatayn, and why does it matter for Babur?
Answer. That Chagatai Turkic was as fit as Persian for high literature. Babur wrote his memoirs in Chagatai.
3How did Bihzad's career connect Timurid Herat with later Safavid and Mughal painting?
Answer. Bihzad worked at Husayn Bayqara's Herat, then headed the Safavid royal library at Tabriz. Safavid painters trained in that tradition (ʿAbd al-Samad, Mir Sayyid ʿAli) founded Mughal painting.
4Which powers took over the Timurids' western and northern territories, and when?
Answer. In the west, the Qara Qoyunlu and then the Aq Qoyunlu (Uzun Hasan's victories of 1467 and 1469), followed by the Safavids from 1501. In the north, the Uzbek Shaybanids (Samarkand 1500–01, Herat 1507).

6Lesson 6

Babur: from Ferghana to Hindustan

1483–1530

Key dates
  1. 14 Feb 1483Babur born at Andijan
  2. 1494Death of ʿUmar Shaykh Mirza; Babur ruler of Ferghana
  3. 1497First capture of Samarkand (held about 100 days)
  4. 1500–01Second capture; defeat at Sar-i Pul; Samarkand lost to Shaybani
  5. 1504Babur takes Kabul
  6. 1507Takes the title pādishāh
  7. 1511–12Third tenure of Samarkand with Safavid help; lost after Ghijduvan
  8. 21 Apr 1526First battle of Panipat; Ibrahim Lodi killed
  9. Mar 1527Battle of Khanwa; Rana Sanga defeated
  10. 1529Battle of the Ghaghra
  11. 26 Dec 1530Babur dies at Agra
Why it matters

Babur lost his Central Asian inheritance and turned the loss into an Indian empire. His Bāburnāma is one of the great autobiographies. At Panipat he combined Ottoman-style carts and guns with the steppe flanking attack, and that victory founded a dynasty that ruled from Delhi and Agra for more than three centuries.

Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur was born on 14 February 1483 at Andijan in the Ferghana valley. He was a fifth-generation descendant of Timur in the male line: Timur, Miran Shah, Sultan Muhammad, Abu Saʿid, ʿUmar Shaykh Mirza, Babur. Through his mother, Qutlugh Nigar Khanum, daughter of Yunus Khan of Moghulistan, he also descended from Chinggis Khan by way of Chagatai. Babur was proud of both lines but thought of himself first and foremost as a Timurid. He was born into the family's last generation in Central Asia, among a dozen quarrelling mīrzās (Timurid princes) with a strong sense of their inheritance and a weak hold on it.

Ferghana and Samarkand lost

In June 1494 Babur's father ʿUmar Shaykh Mirza was killed when a pavilion or dovecote at the fortress of Akhsi collapsed into a ravine. Babur, just eleven, became ruler of Ferghana, surrounded by ambitious uncles and cousins. His overriding goal was Samarkand, the city of Timur. He took it in November 1497 at the age of fourteen, held it for about a hundred days, and lost both Samarkand and his home base of Andijan in the process. In 1500 he took Samarkand again with a small band. In 1501 Muhammad Shaybani Khan defeated him at Sar-i Pul and besieged the city, and Babur had to abandon it. For several years he lived as a landless adventurer in the hills around Ferghana. His memoirs are candid about hunger, humiliation, and near-despair in these years.

Kabul, 1504

In 1504 Babur and his followers crossed the Hindu Kush and took Kabul from the Arghun ruler Muqim. He held it for the rest of his life and grew to love it: its climate, fruit, and gardens, and its position at the crossroads of Central Asia and India. In 1506 he visited Herat after Husayn Bayqara's death and wrote a detailed account of its court. The next year the Uzbeks took the city. In 1507, as the senior surviving Timurid prince, he took the title pādishāh (emperor). In 1511, with the help of Shah Ismaʿil, who had just killed Shaybani, he took Samarkand a third time, but his dependence on the Shiʿi Safavids alienated its Sunni population. After a Safavid army was defeated by the Uzbeks at Ghijduvan in 1512, Babur gave up Transoxiana for good.

The Baburnama

Babur is known to us, as few pre-modern rulers are, through his own words. His memoirs, the Bāburnāma (also called Vaqāyiʿ, "Events"), were written in Chagatai Turkic prose and cover, with gaps, the years 1494 to 1529. They are unusually frank. He records his defeats, his drinking parties and his later renunciation of wine, his adolescent infatuation with a boy in the Andijan bazaar, his judgements on poets and princes, and his observations of plants, animals, and landscapes. His famously sour first impressions of Hindustan are there too: he complained about the lack of good horses, grapes, melons, and running water in gardens, and then went on to catalogue India's fauna and flora with real curiosity. In Wheeler Thackston's English translation it remains one of the great autobiographies. Stephen Dale's The Garden of the Eight Paradises reads it together with Babur's poetry as the self-portrait of a Timurid prince shaped by Persianate culture.

Panipat, 1526

From Kabul, Babur raided into the Punjab from 1519, and he argued that the lands once conquered by Timur were his by right. The Lodi sultanate of Delhi was divided. Its last sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, had alienated powerful Afghan nobles, and Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of the Punjab, invited Babur in. Babur's decisive expedition set out in late 1525. On 21 April 1526 he met Ibrahim at Panipat, north of Delhi. By Babur's own account his force was about 12,000 men, and he estimated the Lodi army at around 100,000, with about a thousand elephants. His numbers may exaggerate the odds. His tactics were a blend of Central Asian and Ottoman practice. He built a barricade of carts chained together "in the Ottoman manner," with gaps for cavalry sorties and positions for matchlockmen and for cannon under his gunner Ustad ʿAli-Quli, and he used the steppe flanking manoeuvre (tulghuma) to envelop the enemy wings. Ibrahim Lodi was killed and his army destroyed. Babur occupied Delhi and Agra within days.

Khanwa, 1527, and the founding of Mughal rule

Panipat gave Babur Delhi but not Hindustan. The strongest power in North India was the Rajput confederacy led by Rana Sanga of Mewar. In March 1527, at Khanwa west of Agra, Babur faced it with an army that was homesick and demoralised. Before the battle he publicly renounced wine, poured out his stock, and framed the campaign as a holy war. Using the same cart-and-gun tactics, he won a decisive victory and took the title ghāzī. The capture of Chanderi in 1528 and victory over the eastern Afghans on the Ghaghra (Gogra) in 1529 extended his rule from Kabul to the borders of Bengal.

Babur died at Agra on 26 December 1530, aged forty-seven. A well-known story says he offered his life to God in exchange for that of his gravely ill son Humayun, walking three times around the sick man's bed. It comes from later court tradition and should be read as pious legend. He was buried first at Agra and later, at his own wish, in a garden on a hillside in Kabul, the Bagh-i Babur.

"Mughal" or Gurkani?

The name "Mughal" (from Persian mughul, "Mongol") was what Indians and, later, Europeans called the new dynasty. It is not what the dynasty called itself, and Babur, who had a low opinion of the Moghul tribesmen of Moghulistan, would not have welcomed it. His house called itself the Gūrkāniyān, "the Gurkanis," from Timur's title güregen, or simply the house of Timur. To Babur and his heirs, India was a Timurid inheritance, won back in the tradition of Timur's raid of 1398.

Key people and terms

Babur ظهیرالدین محمد بابر
Zahir al-Din Muhammad Babur (1483–1530); bābur probably from Persian babr, "tiger."
Bāburnāma بابرنامه
Babur's Chagatai memoirs.
Mīrzā میرزا
From amīrzāda, "son of an amir"; the title of Timurid princes.
Pādishāh پادشاه
Emperor; Babur's title from 1507.
Ibrahim Lodi
Last Lodi sultan of Delhi (r. 1517–26), killed at Panipat.
Rana Sanga
Sangram Singh of Mewar, leader of the Rajput coalition at Khanwa.
Tulghuma
Steppe flanking and encircling manoeuvre.
Gūrkāniyān گورکانیان
"The Gurkanis," the dynasty's own name, from güregen.
Ghāzī غازی
Warrior for the faith; title Babur took after Khanwa.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1Trace Babur's descent from Timur and from Chinggis Khan.
Answer. Timur → Miran Shah → Sultan Muhammad → Abu Saʿid → ʿUmar Shaykh Mirza → Babur. His mother Qutlugh Nigar Khanum was a daughter of Yunus Khan, of the Chagatai (Chinggisid) line.
2Why did Babur ultimately give up on Samarkand and turn south?
Answer. Repeated defeats by Shaybani's Uzbeks, and the failure of his Safavid-backed return in 1511–12 (Ghijduvan) together with Sunni hostility, closed Transoxiana to him. Kabul offered a base facing India.
3Describe the tactics Babur used at Panipat. Which were Central Asian and which Ottoman-derived?
Answer. A chained line of carts with gaps, sheltering matchlockmen and cannon (Ottoman, "Rumi," practice), combined with the steppe tulghuma flanking attack by mounted archers (Central Asian).
4Why is "Gurkani" a more accurate dynastic name than "Mughal"?
Answer. "Mughal" means "Mongol" and was an outsiders' label. The dynasty called itself Gurkani, after Timur's title güregen, stressing Timurid descent.

7Lesson 7

The Timurid legacy in India

1530–1826

Key dates
  1. 1539–40Humayun defeated at Chausa and Kannauj by Sher Shah Sur
  2. Oct 1542Akbar born at Umarkot
  3. 1544Humayun at the court of Shah Tahmasp
  4. 1545Humayun takes Kandahar and Kabul
  5. 1555Victory at Sirhind; Humayun re-enters Delhi
  6. Jan 1556Death of Humayun
  7. Nov 1556Second battle of Panipat; Akbar secure
  8. c. 1570Humayun's tomb completed
  9. 1589Bāburnāma translated into Persian
  10. 1615–19Roe's embassy; Baffin's map (1619)
  11. 1815Elphinstone's Account of the Kingdom of Caubul
  12. 1826Leyden and Erskine's English translation of Babur's memoirs
Why it matters

This lesson explains how a four-year-old conquest became the Mughal Empire. Humayun's Persian exile brought in the painters who founded Mughal art. Akbar turned Timurid descent into imperial ideology, the Mughal provinces became the framework of European maps of India, and a Bāburnāma manuscript from Elphinstone's embassy helped put Babur's own words into English.

Babur left his son an empire that was only four years old, held by a Central Asian army in a country that was still largely hostile. That it survived to become the Mughal Empire, and that it went on calling itself Timurid for three more centuries, owed a great deal to one man's exile in Persia and to his son's genius for turning ancestry into ideology.

Humayun: loss, exile, and return

Nasir al-Din Muhammad Humayun (r. 1530–40 and 1555–56) inherited Babur's empire but not all of its resources. Following Timurid custom, his brothers Kamran, ʿAskari, and Hindal expected shares, and Kamran held Kabul and the Punjab. The real threat was the Afghan leader Sher Khan Sur, who had built a power base in Bihar and Bengal. Sher Khan defeated Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and decisively at Kannauj (Bilgram) in 1540, and ruled North India as Sher Shah. His short reign (1540–45) produced administrative and revenue reforms, a silver coin, the rupiya, and a rebuilt Grand Trunk road, and the Mughals later inherited all of these.

Humayun became a fugitive. In Sind he married Hamida Banu Begum, and their son Akbar was born at Umarkot in October 1542. Refused help by his brothers, Humayun crossed into Iran in 1543–44 and was received by the Safavid Shah Tahmasp at Qazvin. The accounts, including the memoir of Humayun's sister Gulbadan Begum and that of his servant Jawhar, describe both lavish hospitality and heavy pressure. Tahmasp's support apparently came with conditions, including religious gestures towards Shiʿism and the promise of Kandahar. Accounts differ on how far Humayun gave way. With Persian troops he took Kandahar in 1545 and then Kabul from Kamran. He spent a decade fighting his brothers for Afghanistan. After Sher Shah's heirs fell to quarrelling, he re-entered India, won at Sirhind in June 1555, and entered Delhi in July. Six months later, in January 1556, he fell on the stone stairs of his library, the Sher Mandal, and died.

Exile had a cultural payoff. In Iran Humayun met painters of the Safavid royal workshop, heirs of Bihzad's Herat. Two of them, Mir Sayyid ʿAli and ʿAbd al-Samad, joined him in Kabul and became the founders of Mughal painting. Humayun's tomb in Delhi, built after his death under the patronage of his widow and completed around 1570, translated the Timurid domed mausoleum of the Gur-e Amir type into Indian red sandstone and white marble, set in a Persian four-part garden (chahār bāgh). It is the architectural ancestor of the Taj Mahal.

Akbar and the Timurid idea

Akbar (r. 1556–1605) came to the throne at thirteen. In November 1556 his regent Bayram Khan defeated Hemu, the Hindu general who had seized Delhi for the Sur, at the second battle of Panipat. Over the next half-century Akbar built a durable imperial system: the manṣab ranking of nobles, a revenue system based on measurement, alliances with Rajput houses, and a policy of broad religious toleration (ṣulḥ-i kull, "peace with all"). His empire stretched from Kabul and Kandahar to Bengal and into the Deccan.

Akbar was the first Timurid ruler of India born there, and he made a great deal of his Timurid descent. His minister and historian Abu'l-Fazl opened the Akbarnāma with a long genealogy tracing the emperor through Timur back to the Mongol ancestress Alan Qo'a, and he presented the dynasty's light as a divine radiance passed down the generations. The court produced an illustrated history of the dynasty, the Tārīkh-i khāndān-i Tīmūriyya (c. 1580s), now in the Khuda Bakhsh Library, Patna, and illustrated Persian versions of Yazdi's Zafarnāma. In 1589 the Bāburnāma was translated into Persian by ʿAbd al-Rahim Khan-i Khanan, and several lavishly illustrated copies were made. Babur's memoirs became a family scripture. Later emperors kept the thread going. Imperial seals set the reigning emperor's name at the centre of rings listing his ancestors back to Timur, and Shah Jahan styled himself "the Second Lord of the Auspicious Conjunction" (Ṣāḥib-qirān-i thānī), a deliberate echo of Timur.

"Princes of the House of Timur"

The most remarkable object of this dynastic self-image is a large painting on cotton in the British Museum, known as Princes of the House of Timur. It was made around 1550–55, probably in Kabul, at the beginning of Mughal painting, and is attributed to ʿAbd al-Samad (some scholars suggest Mir Sayyid ʿAli). It showed Humayun and his relatives in a garden pavilion. Infrared study has shown that it was repainted several times. Under Jahangir, portraits of Akbar, Jahangir, and his sons were added, and under Shah Jahan, portraits of Shah Jahan and his son Dara Shikoh. It was turned into a gathering of Timur's descendants across generations. The painting shows the dynasty literally painting itself into the house of Timur.

Looking ahead: Europeans map the Mughal empire

After 1600, Europeans increasingly saw India through the frame of the "Great Mogul." The English East India Company, chartered in 1600, sent Sir Thomas Roe as ambassador to Jahangir's court (1615–19). From Roe's information the navigator William Baffin compiled a map of 1619, A Description of East India conteyninge th'Empire of the Great Mogoll. Samuel Purchas printed it in 1625, and it became the basis for English maps of India for decades. Its labels are the provinces (ṣūbas) and cities of the Mughal system that Akbar had organised. In the eighteenth century French and British cartographers, above all Jean-Baptiste Bourguignon d'Anville (Carte de l'Inde, 1752) and James Rennell (Map of Hindoostan, 1782, with its Memoir), still took the Mughal ṣūbas as their framework, even as real Mughal power shrank. For a collector of Indian maps, the Timurid administrative inheritance is literally written on the sheet.

Coda: Elphinstone and Babur's Kabul

In 1808–09 the East India Company sent Mountstuart Elphinstone on an embassy to the Durrani king Shah Shuja. Elphinstone never reached Kabul. Shah Shuja received the mission at Peshawar in 1809. But Elphinstone gathered information systematically from informants, and the mission's surveyor, Lieutenant John Macartney, compiled a map. The result, An Account of the Kingdom of Caubul, and its Dependencies in Persia, Tartary, and India (London, 1815), became the foundational British description of Afghanistan. It is a very different lens on the country Babur had loved three centuries earlier. The Babur connection is direct: at Peshawar Elphinstone acquired a manuscript of the Bāburnāma in the original Turki, and he passed it to William Erskine, who used it to complete John Leyden's English translation, published in 1826 as the Memoirs of Zehir-ed-Din Muhammed Baber. Babur's own voice first reached English readers partly thanks to Elphinstone's embassy.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1How did Humayun's exile in Safavid Iran shape Mughal culture?
Answer. It gained him Safavid troops to recover Kandahar and Kabul, and it brought Safavid painters (ʿAbd al-Samad, Mir Sayyid ʿAli) into his service, the founders of Mughal painting. Persian models also shaped court culture and architecture.
2Give three ways the Mughal court displayed its Timurid descent.
Answer. Any three: the dynastic name Gurkani; Abu'l-Fazl's genealogy in the Akbarnāma; illustrated dynastic histories (Tārīkh-i khāndān-i Tīmūriyya, Zafarnāma copies); Persian translation and illustration of the Bāburnāma; genealogical seals; Shah Jahan's title "Second Sahib-qiran"; the "Princes of the House of Timur" painting.
3What does infrared study reveal about the "Princes of the House of Timur" painting?
Answer. It was painted around 1550–55 and repainted in several phases. Under Jahangir, portraits of Akbar, Jahangir, and his sons were added, and under Shah Jahan, Shah Jahan and Dara Shikoh. The dynasty kept inserting itself into the house of Timur.
4How is Elphinstone's 1808–09 embassy connected to the English translation of the Baburnama?
Answer. At Peshawar in 1809 Elphinstone obtained a Turki manuscript of the memoirs, which William Erskine used to complete Leyden's translation (1826).

Genealogy: Timur to Babur to Akbar

Simplified. It shows only the lines discussed in this course. Shaded boxes are rulers; dates are reigns or lifespans.

Answer key

Lesson 1

  1. Only male-line descendants of Chinggis Khan could legitimately be khan. Timur ruled as amīr, kept puppet Chinggisid khans (Soyurghatmish, then Sultan Mahmud), and married a Chinggisid princess to become güregen, "royal son-in-law."
  2. Moghulistan in the east kept real Chinggisid khans and a more nomadic life. In Transoxiana the tribal amirs held power and the khans were figureheads, especially after Qazaghan killed Qazan in 1346–47.
  3. He submitted to Tughluq Temür and was confirmed in control of Kesh, then used that base to ally with Amir Husayn once the Moghuls withdrew.
  4. Constant campaigns kept the tribal army occupied, rewarded, and loyal to him personally. Conquest held the regime together and kept rivals from turning on him.

Lesson 2

  1. The Kartids (Herat), the Sarbadars (Sabzavar), the Muzaffarids (Shiraz, with Fars, Kirman, and Isfahan), and the Jalayirids (Baghdad and Tabriz).
  2. Isfahan surrendered, then rose at night and killed the Timurid collectors. Timur ordered a massacre and towers of heads. The 70,000 figure comes from the court historian Hafiz-i Abru. It should be credited to him as a chronicler's claim, not treated as a verified count.
  3. It first appears in Dawlatshah Samarqandi's anthology of 1487, a century later. It is too neat and too late to be trusted.
  4. Cities that submitted paid ransom (māl-i amān) and were generally spared. Cities that resisted or rebelled faced massacre and destruction. From both he took treasure and, especially, skilled artisans deported to Samarkand and Kesh.

Lesson 3

  1. After Firuz Shah died in 1388 came a succession crisis, rival sultans, domination by Mallu Iqbal, and provinces such as Jaunpur breaking away.
  2. Yazdi says Timur had the captives killed before the battle, giving 100,000. Treat it as an attested massacre whose size comes from a court panegyric and is uncertain.
  3. Khizr Khan, Timur's appointee, founded it and acknowledged Shah Rukh as overlord. This made Delhi formally a Timurid dependency and strengthened Babur's later claim.
  4. Any three of: Jaunpur (Sharqi), Gujarat, Malwa, Bengal, and in the south the Bahmanis.

Lesson 4

  1. The causes were rival claims over the eastern Anatolian lords and Ottoman sheltering of Timur's enemies such as Qara Yusuf. The most important consequence was the Ottoman Interregnum (1402–13), which delayed the fall of Constantinople by about fifty years.
  2. Both are firsthand outsiders: Ibn Khaldun met and questioned Timur at Damascus, and Clavijo described Samarkand and the aged conqueror in 1404.
  3. His designated heir Pir Muhammad was far away in Kandahar, and Khalil Sultan seized Samarkand. By 1409 Shah Rukh had won out.
  4. A ribbed, melon-shaped dome on a high drum and turquoise tilework, with a dark green jade cenotaph inside. It influenced Humayun's tomb (and, more distantly, the Taj Mahal).

Lesson 5

  1. He built the Samarkand observatory with its giant meridian arc and produced the Zīj-i Sulṭānī with a catalogue of 1,018 stars. He was defeated and put to death on the orders of his son ʿAbd al-Latif in 1449.
  2. That Chagatai Turkic was as fit as Persian for high literature. Babur wrote his memoirs in Chagatai.
  3. Bihzad worked at Husayn Bayqara's Herat, then headed the Safavid royal library at Tabriz. Safavid painters trained in that tradition (ʿAbd al-Samad, Mir Sayyid ʿAli) founded Mughal painting.
  4. In the west, the Qara Qoyunlu and then the Aq Qoyunlu (Uzun Hasan's victories of 1467 and 1469), followed by the Safavids from 1501. In the north, the Uzbek Shaybanids (Samarkand 1500–01, Herat 1507).

Lesson 6

  1. Timur → Miran Shah → Sultan Muhammad → Abu Saʿid → ʿUmar Shaykh Mirza → Babur. His mother Qutlugh Nigar Khanum was a daughter of Yunus Khan, of the Chagatai (Chinggisid) line.
  2. Repeated defeats by Shaybani's Uzbeks, and the failure of his Safavid-backed return in 1511–12 (Ghijduvan) together with Sunni hostility, closed Transoxiana to him. Kabul offered a base facing India.
  3. A chained line of carts with gaps, sheltering matchlockmen and cannon (Ottoman, "Rumi," practice), combined with the steppe tulghuma flanking attack by mounted archers (Central Asian).
  4. "Mughal" means "Mongol" and was an outsiders' label. The dynasty called itself Gurkani, after Timur's title güregen, stressing Timurid descent.

Lesson 7

  1. It gained him Safavid troops to recover Kandahar and Kabul, and it brought Safavid painters (ʿAbd al-Samad, Mir Sayyid ʿAli) into his service, the founders of Mughal painting. Persian models also shaped court culture and architecture.
  2. Any three: the dynastic name Gurkani; Abu'l-Fazl's genealogy in the Akbarnāma; illustrated dynastic histories (Tārīkh-i khāndān-i Tīmūriyya, Zafarnāma copies); Persian translation and illustration of the Bāburnāma; genealogical seals; Shah Jahan's title "Second Sahib-qiran"; the "Princes of the House of Timur" painting.
  3. It was painted around 1550–55 and repainted in several phases. Under Jahangir, portraits of Akbar, Jahangir, and his sons were added, and under Shah Jahan, Shah Jahan and Dara Shikoh. The dynasty kept inserting itself into the house of Timur.
  4. At Peshawar in 1809 Elphinstone obtained a Turki manuscript of the memoirs, which William Erskine used to complete Leyden's translation (1826).

Further reading

Titles, authors, and publication details were checked against publisher, library, or catalogue records in September 2026.

Timur and the Timurids

  • Beatrice Forbes Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (Cambridge University Press, 1989). The standard scholarly study of how Timur built and held his power.
  • Beatrice Forbes Manz, Power, Politics and Religion in Timurid Iran (Cambridge University Press, 2007). Shah Rukh's Iran, government and society.
  • Justin Marozzi, Tamerlane: Sword of Islam, Conqueror of the World (HarperCollins, 2004). Vivid popular biography and travelogue.
  • Ruy González de Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane, 1403–1406, translated by Guy Le Strange (London: Routledge, Broadway Travellers, 1928; reprinted). The eyewitness account of Samarkand in 1404.
  • Thomas W. Lentz and Glenn D. Lowry, Timur and the Princely Vision: Persian Art and Culture in the Fifteenth Century (Los Angeles County Museum of Art / Arthur M. Sackler Gallery, Smithsonian Institution, 1989). The classic exhibition catalogue of Timurid art.

Babur and the Mughals

  • The Baburnama: Memoirs of Babur, Prince and Emperor, translated, edited, and annotated by Wheeler M. Thackston (Modern Library, 2002; first published 1996). The best modern English translation.
  • Stephen F. Dale, The Garden of the Eight Paradises: Babur and the Culture of Empire in Central Asia, Afghanistan and India (1483–1530) (Brill, 2004). A critical biography built on the memoirs and poetry.
  • John F. Richards, The Mughal Empire (The New Cambridge History of India I.5, Cambridge University Press, 1993). A concise standard survey, 1526–1720.
  • Mountstuart Elphinstone, An Account of the Kingdom of Caubul, and its Dependencies in Persia, Tartary, and India (London, 1815). Digitised copies are freely available (e.g. Library of Congress, Internet Archive).

Reference

  • Encyclopaedia Iranica (iranicaonline.org), for example "Isfahan vi. Medieval period," and entries on individual Timurid figures and topics. Encyclopaedia Britannica online entries on Timur, Ulugh Beg, the sack of Delhi (1398), and Babur are reliable short overviews.

Data and map sources

  • Coastlines, rivers and lakes: Natural Earth (naturalearthdata.com, public domain). The maps use 1:50m land, the 1:10m rivers and lake centrelines and 1:10m lakes, plus the 1:10m historic lakes layer for the Aral Sea. The modern Aral lakes, recent reservoirs and the Sarygamysh lake are left out because they did not exist in this form in the period. The rivers are today's courses, and some have shifted since the fifteenth century (the lower Amu Darya among them). All maps use an Albers equal-area conic projection, so areas can be compared by eye.
  • Historical borders: A. Ourednik, historical-basemaps (github.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps, GPL-3.0), layers 1300, 1400, 1492 and 1530, clipped to Natural Earth land. The project warns that its borders are approximate and should be checked against other sources. That is why the lessons' text, not the outlines, carries the argument. The lost-provinces overlay on the Shah Rukh map was built from Natural Earth admin-0/admin-1 units, as its caption explains.
  • City and battle positions: coordinates from English Wikipedia and Wikidata, retrieved in September 2026 (for example Samarkand 39.65° N 66.97° E; Otrar 42.85° N 68.30° E; Panipat 29.39° N 76.97° E). Sarai is placed at the Selitrennoye site on the lower Volga.
  • Empire areas: Rein Taagepera, "Expansion and Contraction Patterns of Large Polities: Context for Russia," International Studies Quarterly 41, no. 3 (1997): 475–504, Appendix tables for the Timurid ("Timur"), Mughal ("Mogul"), Chagatai, Il-Khan, Golden Horde and Delhi series. No other area figures are used.
  • Dates and chronicle figures: as stated in the lessons, with the chronicle source named for every casualty figure.
